implementation_notes: System.Collections.Generic.PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> (added in .NET 6) is the built-in: a min-heap by default, with TryDequeue, Peek, Enqueue, and an UnorderedItems view for O(n) iteration. Being newer than the classic List-based PriorityQueue, it has no priority-tie awareness and no decrease-key, so for a scheduler where fairness matters add a monotonic sequence to the priority tuple. The older SortedSet with a comparer is not a priority queue - it maintains full order at O(log n) per insert with a much bigger constant, and it is the wrong structure when only the extremum is needed.
pitfalls: No decrease-key: mutating the priority of an enqueued item has no effect, and the UnorderedItems view is not a supported way to reach into the heap.
EnumerateUnorderedItems/ UnorderedItems is O(n) and explicitly not ordered - iterating it does not yield sorted output.
A tuple priority without a sequence number ties the comparison and falls through to comparing the payloads, which may not be comparable.
The pre-.NET-6 List-based PriorityQueue has no UnorderedItems view and is noticeably slower; check the target framework before choosing.
